newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Tough UK food market may hit M&S.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Tough UK food market may hit M&S.

text.p: Marks & Spencer Plc is set to produce a respectable increase in overall profits when it reports annual results next Tuesday, but low food price inflation could have made life tough for its food retail business, analysts said.

Britain's biggest clothing chain and retail sector leader is expected to deliver another solid set of results, but food could become a focus if its performance has suffered from the competitive market conditions, analysts said.

The company, which now has stores in Europe and Asia, plus financial services and mail order, is expected to push profits up by about 12 percent for the year to end March 1997. Forecasts range from around 1.10 billion stg to 1.13 billion, up from 993.7 million a year ago. The dividend is expected to rise to about 12.8 pence a share from 11.4 pence last time.

The outlook for clothing was bright until weaker than expected current sales from rival Burton Group Plc on Thursday prompted fears that spring fashion sales in Britain may have been softer than expected, analysts said. But they added that Marks will have the benefit of a buoyant March, plus the Easter holidays.
M&S's shares, which have outperformed the retail sector recently, were hit by the Burton sales figures on Thursday. They were up one penny at 509 by 0805 GMT.
Retail rival Next Plc could make the picture clearer on clothing sales with a current trading update at its annual meeting on Friday.
Retail analysts said food sales may suffer from the fierce battle raging between major food retailers such as J.Sainsbury Plc and Tesco Plc.
"There are worries to the extent that it's a competitive market," said John Richards, retail analyst at NatWest Markets.

Analysts said with food price inflation running significantly below the three percent M&S reported at last year's results, this would mean a reduction in sales unless there were offsetting volume gains. M&S does not compete head on with the major food superstores, but food accounts for about 40 percent of the group's total sales.
In January, M&S said there had been significant price deflation in major areas such as fruit and vegetables.
Richards is estimating a 5.8 percent increase in food sales and a 9.3 percent rise in clothing.
M&S's operations in Europe will see profits hit by the strong pound and higher opening costs, analysts said.
The group warned that costs overall would rise in line with sales when it reported half year results last autumn.
